Trying to Conceive

Menstrual Cycle Phases: What Happens in Each Stage

Updated: August 5, 2026

Written and edited byMohammadamin Namyar, founder of BeMama: checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

The menstrual cycle has four phases: menstruation, the follicular phase, ovulation, and the luteal phase. On a typical 28-day cycle, bleeding covers roughly days 1 to 5, the follicular phase runs from day 1 until ovulation around day 14, and the luteal phase fills the final two weeks. Real cycles range from about 21 to 35 days in adults, and that whole spread is normal. This guide walks through each phase, the hormones behind it, and when cycle length deserves a closer look.

The four phases, in order

Day 1 of your cycle is the first day of full bleeding, not spotting. Menstruation usually lasts about 2 to 7 days while the uterus sheds the lining it built last cycle. The follicular phase starts on that same day 1 and continues until ovulation, so the two overlap. During these days, your brain releases follicle stimulating hormone, which prompts a group of tiny egg-containing sacs called follicles to grow. One follicle becomes dominant, and rising estrogen from it rebuilds the uterine lining. On a textbook 28-day cycle, the follicular phase covers roughly days 1 to 13, but in real life it is the part that stretches or shrinks.

Ovulation is the release of the egg from the dominant follicle. On the 28-day model it lands around day 14, though the real day varies a lot from person to person and cycle to cycle. The egg survives about 12 to 24 hours after release. The luteal phase follows, running from ovulation until the day before your next period, usually about 10 to 16 days. The emptied follicle becomes a small hormone factory called the corpus luteum, which keeps the lining thick in case a fertilized egg arrives. If pregnancy does not happen, hormone levels fall, the lining sheds, and a new cycle begins.

The four hormones, in plain language

Follicle stimulating hormone, or FSH, comes from the pituitary gland at the base of your brain. Its job matches its name: it stimulates follicles in the ovary to start maturing at the beginning of each cycle. Luteinizing hormone, or LH, comes from the same gland and stays low for most of the cycle. When the dominant follicle is ready, LH rises sharply in what is called the LH surge, and ovulation usually follows within about 24 to 36 hours. You do not feel these hormones directly, but their timing sets the timing of everything else in the cycle, which is why clinicians talk about them so much.

Estrogen and progesterone are the two hormones you are more likely to feel. Estrogen rises as the dominant follicle grows. It rebuilds the uterine lining after a period and, at its peak, helps trigger the LH surge. Some people notice more energy around this rise, though experiences vary widely. Progesterone takes over after ovulation. Made by the corpus luteum, it holds the lining in place, warms the body slightly, and can bring the familiar premenstrual heaviness, sore breasts, or lower mood. If no pregnancy starts, progesterone falls after roughly two weeks, and that drop is what starts your next period.

Why day 14 is only an average

The famous 28-day cycle with ovulation on day 14 is a textbook model, not a rule your body signed. Mainstream guidance describes the two halves differently: the luteal phase, the stretch after ovulation, is fairly stable at about 10 to 16 days for most people, while the follicular phase, the stretch before ovulation, is the flexible part. Slow follicle growth one month means later ovulation and a longer cycle. Faster growth means earlier ovulation and a shorter cycle. So the length of your whole cycle mostly reflects how long your body took to get a follicle ready, not how long the second half lasted.

This changes how you estimate ovulation. Instead of counting 14 days forward from your period, it is closer to reality to count back: ovulation tends to happen roughly 10 to 16 days before the next period starts. Someone with 35-day cycles is likely ovulating somewhere around day 19 to 25, well past day 14. Someone with 24-day cycles may ovulate around day 8 to 14. Your most fertile days cluster just before and on ovulation day; our guide to fertile window timing covers how to find and use those days, so this article stays focused on the cycle itself.

What counts as normal, and what counts as irregular

For adults, a cycle anywhere from about 21 to 35 days is generally considered normal, and mainstream guidance treats that whole range as healthy. Only a minority of people run a tidy 28 days every month. In the first few years after periods begin, cycles often run longer and less predictably, and that usually settles with time. Some cycle-to-cycle wobble is expected in adults too: a few days of difference between months is common. Illness, travel, high stress, big weight changes, intense training, breastfeeding, and the years approaching menopause can all shift cycle length without anything being wrong.

Irregular means something more specific than a cycle that is not 28 days. Clinicians generally use the word for cycles that are consistently shorter than about 21 days or longer than about 35, cycles whose length swings widely from month to month, or periods that stop for several months when pregnancy and breastfeeding are not the reason. A single odd cycle after a stressful or sick month rarely means much on its own. If your cycles fit that irregular pattern and you are trying to conceive, it deserves a clinician conversation, and we cover that situation in a separate guide on irregular cycles.

Log a few cycles before drawing conclusions

Before deciding anything about your cycle, gather a little data. Note the first day of each period for two to three cycles, along with roughly how heavy the bleeding was and anything unusual, such as spotting between periods or pain that interrupted your day. A note on your phone, a paper calendar, or the BeMama app all work; what matters is dates you can trust, because memory tends to smooth cycles into a neater pattern than they really follow. With two or three real start dates, you can see your actual cycle length instead of assuming 28, and any pattern you bring to an appointment becomes far more useful.

Some patterns deserve a professional look rather than more tracking. Contact a clinician if your cycles are consistently shorter than 21 days or longer than 35, if your period stops for three months or more and you are not pregnant or breastfeeding, if bleeding soaks through a pad or tampon every hour for more than two hours in a row, or if period pain regularly keeps you from normal life. If that kind of heavy bleeding comes with dizziness, weakness, or fainting, seek urgent care rather than waiting for an appointment. Bring your logged dates with you. This guide is general education, not a diagnosis, and a clinician who can examine you and ask follow-up questions is the right next step for any of these signs.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

Cycle length and ovulation timing vary, so calendar dates and home fertility signs provide estimates rather than proof. Temperature usually rises after ovulation, cervical mucus may change beforehand, and urine tests detect a hormone surge that suggests ovulation may follow.

Sleep disruption, illness, travel, breastfeeding, hormonal contraception, and irregular cycles can make patterns harder to interpret. Combining observations may provide useful context, but no home method confirms fertility or guarantees pregnancy.

How BeMama can help

BeMama can place periods, temperatures, cervical mucus, symptoms, and test results on one timeline. Fertile-window dates are educational estimates and must not be used as contraception.

When to seek help

Contact a healthcare professional for persistently absent, very painful, unusually heavy, or highly irregular periods, or when a medical condition may affect fertility.

Key takeaways

  • The menstrual cycle has four phases: menstruation, follicular, ovulation, and luteal.
  • A normal adult cycle can run anywhere from about 21 to 35 days.
  • The luteal phase stays fairly fixed at about 10 to 16 days; the follicular phase is what varies.
  • Ovulation happens roughly 10 to 16 days before your next period, not always on day 14.
  • Log two to three period start dates before drawing conclusions, and see a clinician about consistently short, long, absent, or very heavy cycles.

Frequently asked questions

How long is a normal menstrual cycle?

For most adults, a normal menstrual cycle lasts anywhere from about 21 to 35 days, counted from the first day of one period to the first day of the next. Teens often have longer and less predictable cycles in the first years after periods begin. A few days of variation between cycles is also normal. Cycles consistently outside that range are worth discussing with a clinician.

What day of my cycle do I ovulate?

Ovulation usually happens about 10 to 16 days before your next period starts, which lands near day 14 only if your cycle is about 28 days long. With a 35-day cycle, ovulation is more likely somewhere around day 19 to 25. The day can also shift from one cycle to the next, so tracking a few cycles gives a better estimate than any fixed number.

Is a 35 day cycle normal?

Yes, a 35-day cycle sits at the long end of the range generally considered normal for adults, which is about 21 to 35 days. It usually means your follicular phase runs longer, so you ovulate later than someone with a shorter cycle. If your cycles regularly stretch beyond 35 days or swing widely, mention it to a clinician, especially if you are trying to conceive.

Why is my cycle longer than 28 days?

A cycle longer than 28 days almost always means your follicular phase, the stretch before ovulation, took longer, because the luteal phase after ovulation stays fairly fixed at about 10 to 16 days. Slower follicle growth is common and usually harmless. Stress, illness, travel, weight changes, and breastfeeding can all lengthen it. Consistently long or unpredictable cycles are worth a clinician conversation.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
